newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Indian port congestion again limits diesel imports.
newsitem.headline: Indian port congestion again limits diesel imports.

text.p: Serious congestions at Indian ports, which cost state-owned Indian Oil Corp (IOC) millions of dollars in demurrage claims by shipowners, is still curbing monthly diesel imports, industry sources said on Monday.
After buying only 255,000 tonnes of high speed diesel in its previous tender for September delivery, IOC bought a mere 120,000 tonnes in its latest tender for October delivery.

Trade sources said the tender was awarded to Dutch oil trading firm Vitol and Kuwaiti-based International Petroleum Group at between $1.98 and $2.05 a barrel over MidEast spot quotes, on a cost-and-freight basis.
The market had earlier expected India to buy as much as one million tonnes of diesel for October to cover shortages after its low September imports.
The market is now waiting for hints that India might issue another tender to supplement its October imports.
Traders familiar with the IOC said as many as 40 to 45 oil vessels were still waiting off India's ports to discharge their cargoes.
They said there were sharp differences in the tender committee, which met on Friday to discuss the the volume of diesel that IOC should take in the October tender.

The strong views were that IOC should not take too much until the congestions were cleared, traders said. The tender committee comprises members from the IOC, the Oil Coordinating Committee, the Finance Ministry and Oil Ministry.
Congestion was particularly heavy at the east coast ports of Madras and Haldia, with ships having to wait between 25 and 38 days to offload.

The situation on the west coast, especially at Kandla, was not so severe with ships having to wait between a week and 10 days. This was due to the efficiency of the 20-inch oil products pipeline from Kandla to the hinterland which helps to move the products more quickly.
Traders said a similar pipeline from Haldia would greatly improve the congestion on the east coast, but they did not see it happening for a while.

The congestion and claims by shipowners for loading and discharge delays at aged ports have long posed problems, but are increasing now as port developments fail to keep pace with rising oil demand, traders said.
Trade sources who have business dealings with IOC estimated that demurrage claims ranged between $10 million and $15 million a month.
Shipping agents estimated monthly demurrage claims to be about $2.2 million at Kandla, $3.0 million at Haldia, $1.5 million at Bombay and $2.0 million at Madras.
The serious congestion this year was caused by heavy buying of diesel during the first eight months of this year which totalled 7.4 million tonnes, traders said.
India's diesel demand is growing at an annual rate of 14.5 percent, the government statistics show.
IOC estimates that demand will grow from 35 million tonnes in 1996/1997 to 54 million tonnes by 2001/2002, and 77 million tonnes by 2006/2007.
